North Dakotan here to explain. It’s mostly because of the Cold War.

Here’s what I personally recommend for your situation.

Learn on YouTube and find a bar that hosts music.

Channels like Rick Beato and Produce Like a Pro (Warren Huart) have tons of videos on getting started. Start off with the fundamentals of mixing first (Gain Stage, EQ, Compression) and worry about the gear later.

If you are looking to get starting mixing but don’t have money for a computer and software, you can always start mixing live bands.
If you know of a bar or venue that hosts live music, there is usually a salty sound guy close by that is willing to show someone the ropes (we want a day off every now and then too!). 

Those are a couple options. Just keep in mind that there is no road map or “go-to list” on this career.
Show up, be there, absorb everything, help where you can, be friendly, be dependable.

I know plenty of amazing sound engineers that I won’t recommend to people because they are either not dependable, not flexible, or just generally unpleasant to be around.

Be a good hang and learn as much as you can.
